The former Shah later died in exile in Egypt in 1980 and is buried at the Al-Rifa'i Mosque.

Mohammad Salimi (; February 2, 1937 – January 30, 2016) was an Iranian military person. He was born in Mashhad, Iran. He was the commander-in-chief of the Iranian Army. He served in the Iran-Iraq War. He began his career in 1955 and resigned in 2005. Salimi was the defense minister in the cabinet of Mir-Hossein Mousavi, replacing Javad Fakoori. He was in office from 1981 to August 1984.

Mohammad Mosaddegh was an Iranian politician. He was elected Prime Minister of Iran from 1951 until 1953. He was also an author, administrator, lawyer, and parliamentarian. On 19 August 1953, Mosaddegh was removed from office by the American Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and Britain's MI6. This was called Operation Ajax in the West. In Iran it is called the 28 Mordad 1332 coup ("Mordad" is the Persian name for a summery month and the coup day was a Wednesday on 19 August 1953). The change in power was one reason for the Iranian Revolution in 1979. Mosaddegh was named man of the year in 1951, by Time magazine. He remains one of the most popular people in Iranian history.

Mohammad Nabi Habibi (, 19 December 1945 – 29 January 2019) was an Iranian politician. He was Secretary-General of the Islamic Coalition Party from 2004 until his death in 2019. He was Mayor of Tehran from 1983 until 1987, lasting 44 months. Habibi died from a heart attack on 29 January 2019 in Tehran, aged 73.

Admiral Mohammad Shariff (Urdu: ايڈمرل محمد شريف; born 1920 – 27 April 2020[[Nishan-e-Imtiaz), was a four-star rank admiral. He was an important figure in the Indo-Pakistani war of 1971. He was the Chief of Naval Staff from 1975 to 1979 and Chairman Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee from 1977 to 1980. Shariff died on 27 April 2020, aged 99.

Mohammad Reza Rezaei Kouchi (; born 23 September 1971) is an Iranian politician who represents Jahrom in the Islamic Consultative Assembly since 2008. He is the head of the civil commission of the parliament.

Mohammad Yazdi (, 2 July 1931 – 9 December 2020) was an Iranian cleric and politician. He was the head of Judiciary System of Iran between 1989 and 1999. In 2015, he was elected to lead Iran's Assembly of Experts. Yazdi was also Chief Justice of Iran from 1989 to 1999. Yazdi was born in Isfahan, Iran. Yazdi died on 9 December 2020 from stomach cancer in Tehran, aged 89.
Mohammad Reza Aref (, born 19 December 1951) is an Iranian engineer, academic and reformist politician. He is the Vice President of Iran since 2024, and previously from 2001 until 2005.

Mohammad Reza Rahimi (, born on 11 January 1949) is an Iranian politician who was first vice president from 13 September 2009 until 3 August 2013. On 15 February 2015, Rahimi was convicted of corruption and was sent to jail at Evin Prison.

Mohammed Ali Salim (1935 – 28 January 2022; ) was a Libyan politician. He was the Acting Chairman of the General National Congress of Libya. He was the oldest member of Libya's first democratically elected legislature until Mohamed Yousef el-Magariaf was appointed permanent chair. In 2012, he was the President of the General National Congress of Libya. Salim died in Tunisia on 28 January 2022, at the age of 87.

Mohammad Reyshahri, also known as Mohammad Mohammadi-Nik, (29 October 1946 – 22 March 2022), was an Iranian politician and cleric. He was the first Minister of Intelligence from 1984 to 1989 in the cabinet of Prime Minister Mir-Hossein Mousavi. Reyshahri was Prosecutor-General of Iran from 1991 until 1993. He was also a Member of the Assembly of Experts from 2016 until his death. Reyshahri was born in Rey, Iran. Reyshahri died on 22 March 2022 in Tehran, Iran at the age of 75.
Mohammad Ibrahim Shtayyeh (born 17 January 1959) is a Palestinian politician, academic and economist. He became prime minister of the Palestinian National Authority in March 2019.

Mohammed Sanusi Barkindo (20 April 1959 – 5 July 2022) was a Nigerian politician. From 1 August 2016 until his death, he was the Secretary General of OPEC. Barkindo died on 5 July 2022 in Abuja, Nigeria from a heart attack at the age of 63.

Mohammad Mokhber Dezfuli (born 26 June 1955) is an Iranian politician who served as the acting President of Iran from 19 May 2024 until 28 July 2024, following the death of President Ebrahim Raisi. He was also the 7th and current first vice president of Iran from 8 August 2021 until 28 July 2024.

Mohammad Abdullah Mohammad Mustafa (born August 26, 1954) is a Palestinian economist and politician. He has been the prime minister of the State of Palestine and the Palestinian National Authority since 2024. Mustafa was the Chairman of the Board of the Palestine Investment Fund (PIF), Senior Economic Advisor to President Mahmoud Abbas and an Independent member of the Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organization before becoming prime minister. He was also deputy prime minister and Minister of National Economy of Palestine.

Mohammad Pakpour (; 2 June 1961 – 28 February 2026) was an Iranian military officer who was the Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) from 13 June 2025 until his death on 28 February 2026 during 2026 Iran War.

Mohammed Zahir Shah (16 October 1914 – 23 July 2007) was the last King (Shah) of Afghanistan. He ruled for four decades, from 1933 to 1973. Mohammed Zahir Shah became king of Afghanistan at the age of nineteen after the assassination of his father in November 1933. Since he was so young, his uncle, Shah Mahmood Khan ran the government. Mohammed Zahir Shah took control and was able to keep Afghanistan’s neutral position in international politics. In July 17, 1973, Mohammed Zahir Shah was no longer king after a bloodless coup. He died on 23 July 2007.

Mohammed bin Hammam (Arabic: محمد بن همّام; born 8 May 1949) is a Qatari who used to be a football administrator and the AFC President (1 August 2002 to 14 June 2011). During the 2022 FIFA World Cup bidding, Mohammed bin Hammam was rumored to have bribed officials, so that Qatar can host.

Mohammed Karim Lamrani (1 May 1919 – 20 September 2018) was the Prime Minister of Morocco three times. Lamrani was one of the oldest former living world leaders until his death. Lamrani was born in Fes on 1 May 1919. Lamrani served as the Prime Minister three times: from 6 August 1971 to 2 November 1972, then from 30 November 1983 and 30 September 1986 and lastly from 11 August 1992 to 25 May 1994. Lamrani died on 20 September 2018 at the age of 99.

Mohammed bin Faisal Al Saud (1934 – 14 January 2017) was a Saudi Arabian businessman and a member of the House of Saud. He was the son of King Faisal of Saudi Arabia and one of the early pioneers in the development of Islamic banking. He was born in Taif, Saudi Arabia. Prince Mohammed served as the chairman of the board of trustees of the King Faisal Foundation. He was also a founding board member and trustee of Effat University. Prince Mohammed bin Faisal died on 14 January 2017 in Mecca, Saudi Arabia at the age of 82.

Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud (; born 31 August 1985) is currently the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia, first deputy Prime Minister of Saudi Arabia. He is the youngest minister of defense in the world. He was named the Prime Minister of Saudi Arabia in September 2022. Mohammed is also chief of the House of Saud. He is the leader of the Council for Economic and Development Affairs. He is sometimes described as the power behind the throne of his father, King Salman. Mohammed bin Salman was appointed Crown Prince in June 2017. Muhammad bin Nayef removed himself from all positions. It made Mohammad the heir apparent to the throne. Mohammed has brought a series of social and economic changes since he was appointed in 2017. He lowered the power of the Wahhabi religious group by controlling the powers of the religious police and making women's rights better. He got rid of the ban on female drivers in 2018. He weakened the male-guardianship system in 2019. His Saudi Vision 2030 program aims to reduce the economy's reliance on oil. He wants to do this by investing in non-oil sectors like technology and tourism. The economy still depends on oil. Mohammed's international image is complex. Some in the Western world think he is good for the modernization of Saudi Arabia. They agree with the big plans for the kingdom, like the 2030 Vision. They also think he is a human rights violator. In foreign politics, Mohammed led the Saudi participation in the war in Yemen and made closer relations with Russia, China and Iran. Mohammed announced the launch of Vision 2030 on April 25, 2016. It is a big part of Saudi Arabia's plan to have economic growth. It specifically decreases oil as a main source of money. It also wants economic developments in a lot of different areas. The vision was built around a vibrant society, a strong economy, and an ambitious nation. The 2030 Vision is about making a society where the citizens have a good quality of life. The plan wants to do this by making the healthcare, education, and social services better. The 2030 vision also wants to make a strong and growing economy for the kingdom. It wants to do this by having a lot of different economic areas. It will also make tourism and technology better for the country. The 2030 vision is about making Saudi Arabia an important country in the world. It will do this by raising Saudi Arabia as a leader in things like energy, finance, and culture. The country wil also work with other nations to deal with global challenges. Mohammad bin Salman thinks Saudi Arabia should adopt a moderate kind of Islam. He gave a television speech about it on Ramadan. Bin Salman said that Islam in Saudi Arabia’s harsh views stops his plans for modernization. He also likes events that used to be considered bad. Some of these are live music performances, festival, and sports competitions. Hundreds of citizens have been arrested in the kingdom since 2017. Some of these are social media influencers, journalists, clerics, and tycoons. A few of bin Salman’s cousins were also arrested. Seven activists were arrested in May 2018, including Eman al-Nafjan and Loujain al-Hathloul. Human Rights Watch claimed bin Salman is responsible for the arrests. They also say he is spreading fear to those who don't like his agendas. bin Salman was accused of being a part of killing of The Washington Post journalist Jamal Khashoggi. A lot of countries really didn't like it. He later talked to the American Television program 60 Minutes and said it wasn't true. Mohammad bin Salman wants the Kingdom to be more important in the region. He started to show this power against Iran and the war in Yemen. The Houthis conquered the Yemeni capital Sana’a in September 2014. This made President Hadi leave the country. The Saudis led the group of Arab states to bring him back to power. Hadi used article 51 of the UN Charter to ask for help. The Houthis are close with Iran, who is Saudi Arabia’s rival in the region. Saudi Arabia led the Arab group. It had Egypt, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Sudan and Morocco. Only Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are still really included in the conflict. The Saudis thought it would be a quick invasion, but they learned that it would not be easy. Under President Obama the US agreed with the Arab states but did not help them. The US helped more under President Trump. The Houthis and Iran were not allies before the invasion. They became very good friends because of the war. Iran wanted the war to end because it would make them stronger. The Saudis stayed in the war even though it was expensive. The Saudis are bombing north Yemen, and the United Arab Emirates help the group in south Yemen. As of 2023, the Saudis and Houthis are talking about peace. They are getting closer to ending the war. Under bin Salman rule Saudi Arabia and Russia are allies in the OPEC+, Saudi Arabia is also investing in Russia, this also leads to better relations between the two. This relation has not changed since the 2022 conflict in Ukraine, with $500 million being invested in Gazprom, Rosneft and Lukoil after the conflict had already started even though western countries put sanctions on these companies. When President Trump got to power the relations between the US and Saudi Arabia were bad, President Obama had pressured Saudi Arabia for diplomacy with Iran and to rely less on the US for defense. President Trump was just like Mohammed in its view of Iran as the greatest danger in the Middle East, and also disagreed with Obama’s policy in the Middle East. President Trump let other countries do their internal affairs without pressuring on human rights for example, which is convenient for Mohammed as human rights or not very good in Saudi Arabia. As President Trump saw Iran as the biggest danger in the Middle East he saw the Houthis as Iranian puppets and thus supported and assisted the Saudi invasion. President Trump also spread confusion about the CIA report on the killing of Kashoggi about him doubting if Mohammed really gave the order to kill and sold weapons to Saudi Arabia. When President Biden was still campaigning for president he said he would treat the bin Salman as the pariah Biden called bin Salman because of the poor human rights situation, and the killing of journalist Kashoggi. One of President Biden's first acts as president was releasing the CIA report that blamed bin Salman of giving the order to kill Kashoggi, and before the report was published, President Biden called with King Salman saying he is the King and official leader of the country and not bin Salman, the Saudis rejected the report. Biden also paused the sale of ammunition to the Saudi Arabia any more lowering relations with Saudi Arabia. In 2022 and 2023 the OPEC started producing less oil leading to bad reactions from the Biden administration. The relations between Saudi Arabia and China are good as China is Saudi Arabia’s largest trading partner and with large investments such as an Aramco joint venture of $10 billion and 35 other investments worth $28 billion in total. China did not blame Mohammed bin Salman for the murder of Khashoggi and for the human suffering in Yemen and Saudi Arabia stays silent or says China has the right to defend itself or to fight ‘terrorism’ as the way China treats its Muslim Uighur minority. That Saudi Arabia’s relation with China is good was also visible in the diplomatic deal that Saudi Arabia made with Iran in talks in China. After the Iranian revolution in 1979, a rivalry between Saudi Arabia and Iran over the leadership over the Islamic world emerged, and after Iran tried to export revolution over the region Saudi Arabia feared a revolution. It led to a rivalry but in 2011 this rivalry became much harder as uprising in the region led to the two supporting opposite sides in conflicts. In 2016 after a Shi’ite cleric Sheik Nimr al-Nimr was executed by Saudi Arabia after demonstrations and the storming of the Saudi Embassy in Tehran by protesters, this led to the cut of diplomatic ties between the two. In 2023 an unexpected deal between the two was signed after diplomatic talks hosted by China, in which they would again open their embassies, bin Salman likely made this deal to support his Vision 2030 and the relation with Iran was an obstacle for foreign investment.

Mohammed Mahdi Akef (July 12, 1928 – September 22, 2017) was the head of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Egypt-based Islamic political movement, from 2004 until 2010. He assumed the post, that of "general guide" (frequently translated as "chairman") upon the death of his predecessor, Ma'mun al-Hudaybi. Akef was arrested on 4 July 2013. On 14 July 2013 Egypt's new prosecutor general Hisham Barakat ordered his assets to be frozen. Akef died on 22 September 2017 in Cairo of sepsis at the age of 89.

Mohammed VI (; born 21 August 1963) is the King of Morocco. He became king on 23 July 1999 after the death of his father, King Hassan II. In 2015, he was estimated by Forbes magazine to be worth US$5.8 billion, and the Moroccan Royal Family has one of the largest fortunes in the world. 21 August 1963-23 July 1999: His Royal Highness The Crown Prince of Morocco 23 July 1999-present: His Majesty The King of Morocco The revolutionary wave that took over the Arab World in 2011, called the Arab Spring, had also an impact on Morocco. The lack of trust in the political class because of corruption allegations has made the population eager for change. Furthermore the powers granted to the monarch, by the constitution, regarding the appointment of high officials such as the prime minister have represented an issue for the democratization of the regime. Therefore the crown has named a so-called Commission Consultative pour la Re´vision Constitutionnelle (CCRC) with the purpose of framing a new constitution that would limit the power of the monarch and increase the ones of the elected representatives. The civil society, made out of the most important political parties, trade unions, and media, has encouraged the voters to vote “yes”. On the 1 July 2011 the referendum for the constitution passed with an overwhelming majority, 98.5% voting in favor of the new constitution. One of the voters was King Mohammed VI himself. According to the new constitution the monarch would be forced to appoint the head of government from the ranks of the party that received the most votes. The prime-minister would not only receive the title of president of the government, but would also gain executive powers such as implementing laws. This shift of executive powers from the King to the elected officials marks a significant turning point towards a constitutional monarchy. The judiciary, usually criticized for the lack of independence, has also gained significant autonomy. As promised by the king, the crown would no longer interfere in the criminal justice system. These changes were embraced, on the international stage, by the Obama administration and the European Union. However the monarch would still hold important titles within the state such as the head of state, head of the armed forces, and protector of the Islamic faith in Morocco. The early years of the reign of king Mohammed VI saw a stagnation of the issue of Western Sahara. Furthermore the U.N. wanted to organize a referendum in the region that would determine the status of the territory. However, since 2007 Morocco has managed to shift the wind in its favor and after the U.N. Security Council adopted Resolution 1754, it was made clear that a referendum was no longer viable. The government from Rabat has proposed a decentralized form of governance, with the territory still being under the crown’s sovereignty. Only a few days before leaving office in 2020, President Donald Trump signed a Joint Declaration between Morocco, the United States, and Israel. This normalized Moroccan-Israeli ties and the United States formally recognize Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara. The US began to formally support Morocco’s autonomy plan as the sole basis for resolving the long-standing Western Sahara conflict. This recognition marked a significant American policy shift. Since then, Morocco has gained significant regional and international support for its sovereignty over Western Sahara, with influential states and several European countries, which include Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Serbia, Hungary, Cyprus and Romania, backing its autonomy initiative. The unwavering U.S. stance and European endorsements have strengthened Morocco’s diplomatic position and partnerships.

Muhammad Nadir Shah (, – born Muhammad Nadir Khan; 9 April 1883 – 8 November 1933) was King of Afghanistan from 15 October 1929 until his assassination in November 1933. Previously, he served as Minister of War, Afghan Ambassador to France, and as a general in the military of Afghanistan. He and his son Muhammad Zahir Shah, who succeeded him, are part of the Musahiban.

Mohammed Nasim (2 April 1948 – 13 June 2020) was a Bangladeshi Awami League politician. Nasim was born in the Sirajganj District in Bangladesh. He was the Minister of Health and Family Welfare from 2014 to 2019. He was Minister of Home Affairs from 1996 to 2001. He has been a member of the Jatiya Sangsad since 2014. He was in the Jatiya Sangsad before from 1986 to 1988 and again from 1991 to 2006. On 1 June 2020, Nasim was hospitalized in Dhaka after testing positive for COVID-19. Four days later, he suffered a cerebral hemorrhage during his treatment. On 13 June 2020, Nasim died while being treated for COVID-19 at a hospital in Dhaka.

Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum (; Muḥammad bin Rāshid al Maktūm; born 15 July 1949) is a politician. He was the acting President of the United Arab Emirates, Vice President and Prime Minister of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and ruler of the Emirate of Dubai. He is responsible for the growth of Dubai into a global city, as well as the launch of a number of major enterprises including Emirates Airline, DP World, and the Jumeirah Group. Many of these are held by Dubai Holding, a company with multi-diversified businesses and investments. Sheikh Mohammed has overseen the development of numerous projects in Dubai including the creation of a technology park and a free economic zone, Dubai Internet City, Dubai Media City, the Dubai International Finance Centre, the Palm Islands and the Burj Al Arab hotel. He also drove the construction of Burj Khalifa, the tallest building in the world.

Mohammed Ibrahim Jega (born June 15, 1981) is an entrepreneur and technology startup founder. He is well known as the chief business development officer at the online payment processing gateway VoguePay. Jega was born in Kaduna state, Nigeria. He holds a bachelor's degree in business administration from the Ahmadu Bello University (ABU), Zaria, in 2003.

Mohammed Bello Adoke (born 1 September 1963) is a Nigerian lawyer, Senior Advocate of Nigeria and was Attorney General of Nigeria and Minister of Justice during the administration President Goodluck Jonathan.

Mohammed Yousef el-Magariaf (also written as Magariaf, Elmegaryaf or Almegaryaf) or, as he writes on his official website, Dr. Mohamed Yusuf Al Magariaf (; born 1940), is a Libyan politician. He was the President of the General National Congress from its first meeting in August 2012 until his resignation in May 2013.

Mohammed al-Khamis ben Yusef ben Hassan al-Alawi, also known as Sidi Mohammed ben Yusef or Mohammed V (10 August 1909 – 26 February 1961), was Sultan of Morocco from 1927 to 1953. He became Sultan again after his return from exile in 1955. He was King from 1957 to 1961.

Mohammed Ahmed bin Sulayem or Mohammed ben Sulayem (; born 12 November 1961) is an Emirati former rally driver. He is the president of the FIA (Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile) since 2021. He was one of the most successful Arab drivers in motor sport history, earning 14 FIA Middle East Rally Championship titles. In 1991, Sulayem founded the UAE Desert Challenge.

Mohammed Shia' Al Sudani is an Iraqi Arab politician who was the Prime Minister of Iraq from 28 October 2022 until 14 May 2026. He previously served as the Human Rights Minister of Iraq under Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, from 2010 until October 2014. He was the Governor of Maysan Province between 2009 and 2010. Sudani was born to Shia parents in Baghdad in 1970. He is married and has four sons. Sudani holds a bachelor's degree from the University of Baghdad in Agricultural Science and a master's degree in Project Management. In 2004, Sudani was appointed as the Mayor of Amarah City. In 2005 he was elected as a member of Maysan Province Council. He was reelected again in 2009 and served until 2010. Later in 2010, he became the minister for human rights. He was succeeded by Mohammed Mahdi Ameen al-Bayati in October 2014, when the government of Haider al-Abadi was formed. In a bid to end the 2022 Iraqi political crisis, the coordination framework officially nominated al Sudani for the post of prime minister.

Mohammed Shahabuddin (born 10 December 1949) is a Bangladeshi lawyer and politician who served as the 16th President of Bangladesh from 2023 until 2026. He was a member of the Awami League until 2024. Before being elected president, he was a judge and commissioner of the Anti-Corruption Commission from 2011 to 2016. On 24 July 2026, Shahabuddin resigned as president due to bad health caused by heart disease, and diabetes.

Mohammed Salim Basindawa (; born 4 April 1935) is a Yemeni politician. He was the Prime Minister of Yemen from 10 December 2011 to 24 September 2014. He resigned on the same day that Houthi rebels captured Sana'a, the capital of Yemen.

Mohammed al-Bashir (born 1983) is a Syrian engineer and politician. He became the 70th prime minister of Syria and the Prime Minister of the Syrian Transitional Government on 9 December 2024. He has also been the Prime Minister of the Syrian Salvation Government since 13 January 2024.

Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani (; born 1 November 1980) is a Qatari economist, and politician who has the Prime Minister of Qatar since 7 March 2023. He has been the Minister of Foreign Affairs since 2016. He has also been serving as Chairman of the Qatar Fund for Development (QFFD) since 2014. He is a member of Qatar's Supreme Council for Economic Affairs and Investments (SCEAI) since 2014. He was the country's deputy prime minister from 2017 to 2023 and was chairman of the Qatar Investment Authority from 2018 to 2023.

Peter Mohan Maithree Peiris, PC is a Sri Lankan lawyer. He was the Attorney General of Sri Lanka from 2008 to 2011 and was the de facto Chief Justice of Sri Lanka from 2013 to 2015 when President Maithripala Sirisena made his appointment void in 2015.

Mohan Sanjibhai Delkar (19 December 1962 – 22 February 2021) was an Indian politician. He was elected seven times as a member of Lok Sabha (parliament) from Dadra and Nagar Haveli from 1989 to 2009 and from 2019 until his death. He was a member of the Bharatiya Janata Party. Delkar was born in Silvassa, Dadra and Nagar Haveli. Delkar died on 22 February 2021 in Mumbai, Maharashtra at the age of 58. The cause of death was suicide.

Mohsen Abdel Hamid (born 1937 ) is an Iraqi politician and Islamic scholar who was a member of the Interim Iraq Governing Council. He was president of the council in February 2004. He was a member of the President of the Governing Council of Iraq as the 42nd Prime Minister of Iraq. On 30 May 2005, Abdel Hamid was arrested by accident by U.S. troops.

Moin Nawaz Warraich (; born 22 February 1949) is a retired army officer and politician and the member of the Provincial Assembly of the Punjab since May 2013. Moin Nawaz Warraich is one of the few Politicians who is very honest and is highly respected even by his oposition party members. He comes from a very well respected families of Gujarat. He is the Son of Ch Gun Nawaz Warraich and the Grand Son of Ch Muzaffar Khan Warraich. Warraich was born on 22 February 1949 in Gujrat to Gul Nawaz Warraich. He completed his education from Pakistan Military Academy in 1970. Warraich is a Pakistan Army officer and has served as a Major until his retirement in 1995.

Mohsin Ahmad Alaini (20 October 1932 – 25 August 2021) was a Yemeni politician. He was the Prime Minister of the Yemen Arab Republic five times between 1967 and 1975. Al-Aini was the first Foreign Minister of the Yemen Arab Republic. Al-Aini died on 25 August 2021 in Cairo, Egypt at age 88.

Mohsen Fakhrizadeh Mahabadi (; 195827 November 2020) was an Iranian nuclear physicist. He was a professor of physics at Imam Hussein University in Tehran. As the victims of the killing of Iranian nuclear scientists, he was murdered in the ambush on November 27, 2020. He also was a brigadier general in the Iranian Revolutionary Guard, senior scientist in the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics and the former head of the Physics Research Center (PHRC) at Lavizan-Shian. Fakhrizadeh was believed by many countries as being in charge of Iran's nuclear programme, Project 111, which tried to help the country create a nuclear bomb. On 27 November 2020, Fakhrizadeh was shot and killed while traveling in a car near Tehran. After he was fatally shot, the attack began when a truck carrying explosives hidden under a load of wood exploded near his car. His three bodyguards were also killed before the bomb attack. He was 62 years old. Another car was also exploded and destroyed.

Ayatollah Mohsen Mojtahed Shabestari (; 1937 – 17 November 2021) was an Iranian Shiite cleric and politician. He was born in Shabestar, Iran. He was a member of the Islamic Consultative Assembly between 1980 until 1988 and again from 1992 until 2000. He was also a member of the Assembly of Experts between 1983 until his death. Shabestari died on 17 November 2021 in Tehran, Iran from cardiac arrest.

Moira Deeming is an Australian politician. She serves on the Legislative Council (upper house) for the Australian state of Victoria with the Liberal Party. Deeming was removed from the Liberal Party for nine months because she spoke at an anti-transgender rally. The National Socialist Network also attended the meeting on their own and were seen giving the Nazi salute. Deeming said that she does not like Nazis so she was suspended for 9 months instead of being removed. On 4 May 2023, Deeming said that she would sue Victorian Liberal Party leader John Pesutto if he does not say that she is not a Nazi. On 12 May 2023, the party voted 19 to 11 to remove her. She is of Māori descent and is a Presbyterian. She has four children.

Moilangpok Punshiba (also spelled Moirangpok Punshiba) was a king of the Khuman dynasty who ruled from 350 CE to 400 CE. He was a contemporary of the Meitei king Pengshiba, who ruled the Ningthouja dynasty from 378 CE to 393 CE.

Mohsin Naqvi, is a Pakistani politician who is current 40th Interior Minister of Pakistan since 11 March 2024. He was included in cabinet of Shehbaz Sharif and appointed as Interior Minister of Pakistan.

Moïse Katumbi Chapwe (; born 28 December 1964) is a Congolese politician who served as Governor of Katanga Province from 2007 to 2015. He was one of the contenders to succeeded by Joseph Kabila in the run up to the 2018 election but he was barred from returning and entering the country to file in his nomination for the presidency. In December 2021, Moïse Katumbi officially launched his political party in view of the 2023 presidential election.

Moisés Torres (1949 – 4 August 2021) was a Bolivian politician, journalist, and professor. He was a member of Conscience of Fatherland. He represented the Chuquisaca Department in the Chamber of Deputies from 1997 to 2002. Torres was born in Sucre, Bolivia. Torres died on 4 August 2021 in Sucre of COVID-19, aged 72.
Moisés Omar Halleslevens Acevedo (born 4 September 1949) is a Nicaraguan politician. He was the Vice President of Nicaragua during the third term of President Daniel Ortega from 2012 until 2017.

Mokgweetsi Eric Keabetswe Masisi (born 21 July 1961) is a Botswana politician. He became the fifth President of Botswana in 2018. He has also became Minister of Education in 2014. He was Minister of Presidential Affairs and Public Administration from 2011 to 2014. He was first elected to Parliament in 2009.

Mokhtar Hashim (1 May 1942 – 17 November 2020) was a Malaysian politician. From 1981 to 1983, he was the Minister for Culture, Youth, and Sports in Mahathir Mohamad's Cabinet. Hashim died on 17 November 2020 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia at the age of 78.

Moktar Ould Daddah ( Mukhtār Wald Dāddāh; December 25, 1924 – October 14, 2003) was the President of Mauritania from 1960, when his country gained its independence from France, to 1978, when he was removed in a military coup d'etat. He died in Paris after a long-illness on October 14, 2003 at the age of 78.
Mokdad Sifi (; born 21 April 1940) is an Algerian politician. Sifi was Head of Government of Algeria from 11 April 1994 to 31 December 1995. In 1999, he unsuccessfully ran for President of Algeria.

Mokhzani Mahathir (born 2 January 1961) is a businessman from Malaysia. He used to work in Kedah UMNO but stopped being involved in politics now. Mokhzani is the second oldest son of the ex-Prime Minister of Malaysia, Mahathir Mohamad.

Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei (born 8 September 1969) is an Iranian politician and cleric who has been the third Supreme Leader of Iran since 8 March 2026. He is the second oldest child of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Khamenei served in the Iran–Iraq War from 1987 to 1988. Khamenei was born in Mashhad into the Azeri–Persian Khamenei family. He was nine when his father emerged as a leading figure in the Iranian Revolution. He studied in Sardasht and Mahabad, and graduated high school from Tehran and Islamic theology. Khamenei joined the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in 1987 and was in the Iran–Iraq War. In 1999, he continued his studies in Qom to become a cleric, and joined the Qom Seminary as a theological teacher afterwards. He took control of the Basij paramilitary volunteer militia in 2009. Mojtaba Khamenei was seen as one of the likely candidates to replace his father as the new Supreme Leader following his father's assassination. Mojtaba Khamenei was seen as the favorite candidate by the IRGC. Khamenei himself was a target in the middle strikes that killed his father, wife and children, however he survived because he was out in the garden seconds before his father’s home was attacked. When the Supreme Leader election took place in early March, several council members were against Khamenei's candidacy. including eight who stated that they would boycott a second online electoral meeting planned for 5 March. On 5March 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump said that he did not support Khamenei becoming supreme leader. On 8 March 2026, the 88-person Assembly of Experts announced that Khamenei was elected Supreme Leader. Unlike other supreme leaders or cleric leaders, Khamenei never led a sermon in public, ran for public office, or had a major clerical leadership role before becoming supreme leader. Mojtaba teaches theology in the Qom Seminary. He married Zahra Haddad-Adel, a daughter of Gholam-Ali Haddad-Adel, in 1999. Their first child was born in 2007. The first son is Mohamed Amin, followed by daughter Fatemeh Sadaat, and second son Mohamed Bagher. His wife, his parents, and one of his sons were killed in the 2026 US–Israeli strikes. Khamenei taught theology in the Qom Seminary; from 2004 he taught Kharij-e Fiqh (advanced jurisprudence) courses for approximately two decades and was considered the instructor of one of the most heavily attended advanced seminary classes. The Dars-e Kharij is the highest level of jurisprudential instruction and a prerequisite for attaining the rank of mujtahid, a scholar qualified to perform independent legal reasoning (ijtihad) in Islamic law.

Willem Jacob "Molly" Geertsema (18 October 1918 - 27 June 1991) was a Dutch civil servant and politician. He was a member of the People's Party for Freedom and Democracy (VVD). Geertsema was a member of the House of Representatives (parliamentary leader) and the Senate. He was also a deputy prime minister, government minister, political leader, councillor (Leiden and The Hague), mayor (Warffum and Wassenaar) and Queen's Commissioner of Gelderland. Geertsema, who belonged to the Remonstrants, studied law at Leiden University and was also a lobbyist and LGBT rights activist. He was born in Utrecht and died in Wassenaar at the age of 72.

Molly Gray (born March 18, 1984) is an American attorney and politician. She is a member of the Democratic Party. She was the 83rd lieutenant governor of Vermont from 2021 to 2023. She is the fourth woman to serve as Vermont's lieutenant governor. In December 2021, Gray announced that she would be a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in 2022. She lost the Democratic nomination in August 2022 to Becca Balint.

Momir Bulatović (Cyrillic: Момир Булатовић; 21 September 1956 – 30 June 2019) became the first President of Montenegro in 1990 and was president until 1998. He was also Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (1998–2000). Bulatović died on 30 June 2019 in Raći, Podgorica, Montenegro from a heart attack at the age of 62.

Lt. Gen. Mompati Sebogodi Merafhe (6 June 1936 – 7 January 2015) was a Botswanan politician. He was Vice-President of Botswana from 2008 to 2012. He was a Lieutenant-General and was Botswana's Minister of Foreign Affairs from 1994 to 2008.

Momčilo Krajišnik (; 20 January 1945 – 15 September 2020) was a Bosnian Serb politician. Along with Radovan Karadžić, he co-founded the Bosnian Serb nationalist Serb Democratic Party (SDS). Between 1990 and 1992, he was speaker of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska. Between June and December 1992, he was member of the expanded Presidency of Republika Srpska. After the Bosnian War, he was elected Serb member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the September 1996. In 2006, Krajišnik was found guilty of committing crimes against humanity during the Bosnian War (1992–95) by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) and was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment. H Krajišnik was hospitalized in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska with COVID-19. He died on 15 September 2020 from the infection, aged 75.

Momčilo Gavrić (Serbian: Момчило Гаврић; about 01 May 1906 28 April 1993) was a Serbian child soldier, and the youngest Serbian soldier to serve during both the Serbian Campaign and World War I at just 8 years old, and was even awarded the Commemorative Medal of the Great Serbian Retreat for participating in the Great Serbian Retreat and walking across the mountains of Albania with the rest of the Royal Serbian Army during the harsh and brutal winter of 1915-1916. Momčilo Gavrić also served in the Royal Yugoslav Army during the World War II when Yugoslavia was invaded and occupied by Nazi Germany; he was subsequently also a Nazi concentration camp survivor and a survivor of the prisons of the Yugoslav Communist authorities where he was tortured and labeled as a "enemy of the people" after World War II. Momčilo Gavrić (Serbian: Момчило Гаврић) was born on or around 01 May 1906 to a Serbian peasant family in the rural forest village of Trbušnica near the slopes of Mount Gučevo (or according to his military certificate in the nearby town of Banja Koviljača), in the northwestern Kingdom of Serbia (in the modern-day Loznica Municipality, Mačva District, Republic of Serbia). Momčilo was the eighth of eleven children of Alimpije Gavrić and his wife, Jelena "Elena" Gavrić. After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, on 28 June 1914 in Sarajevo (back then in Austria-Hungary) by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb, Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia for the assaination of the archduke and invaded Serbia the next month on 28 July, thus starting both the Serbian Campaign and World War I. Following the invasion, Momčilo Gavrić's two elder brothers Bogozav and Svetozar Gavrić were drafted into the Royal Serbian Army and were subsequently sent to the frontline with their unit to fight against the Austro-Hungarian Army; Momčilo Gavrić's eldest sister got married and subsequently left the family to live with her husband in Banja Koviljača, a nearby town located about 3 miles northwest of the village of Trbušnica. During the first invasion of Serbia of July-August 1914, Austro-Hungarian soldiers initiated their offensive in invading and occupying western Serbia in their attempts to reach Belgrade, the capital city of Serbia; during their offensive, the Austro-Hungarian troops committed brutal mass murders and atrocities against many of the Serbian civilians living there and destroyed their houses and villages; during the atrocities, sometime between 12 and 15 August 1914, Austro-Hungarian troops occupied the village of Trbušnica (where Momčilo Gavrić lived with his family) and, the same day, they commited a brutal massacre in the village; during the massacre, Momčilo Gavrić's father, mother, three sisters, four of his seven brothers, and grandmother, in addition to many people from the village, were brutally tortured, maimed, and hanged by ethnic "Swabian" Croat Austro-Hungarian soldiers belonging to the Croatian 42nd Home Guard Infantry Division (also nicknamed the "Devil's Division"), who commited the massacres in the village while reportedly drunk and intoxicated. In addition to the massacring many of the inhabitants of the village, the Austro-Hungarian troops also arrested and deported eight men from the village of Trbušnica and sent them across the border to Sarajevo in Austria-Hungary where they were held in internment camps, including – according to some sources – one of Momčilo Gavrić's own relatives. Eight-year-old Momčilo Gavrić solely managed to survive the massacre of his family and village, because he was not in the village when the massacre took place – just several hours before the Austro-Hungarian soldiers entered the village and commited the massacre, his father had sent his son Momčilo to his paternal uncle Vladimir who lived in another village to borrow a ox and a cart, a rug, some food and water, among other supplies, so that he could escape with his family after Austro-Hungarian troops were approaching and heading towards the direction of the village and the neighboring areas and especially after he heard the local rumors from people in neighboring villages that Austro-Hungarian soldiers were killing Serbian civilians and destroying houses and villages in the nearby Mačva and the Pocerina regions of Serbia under their occupation; when Momčilo Gavrić later returned to his village and home after failing to get ox, cart, and supplies from his uncle, he discovered and saw the brutal scene of the massacre in his village; he saw the mutilated body of his father hanging from a tree, and the mutilated bodies of his mother, siblings, and grandmother covered in blood and laying in the yard, as well as the mutilated bodies of many other people in the village; his house was also set on fire. Momčilo Gavrić then discretely saw that the Croatian Austro-Hungarian soldiers who commited the brutal massacre and killed his family and many of the people in his village, were loitering and drinking strong rakija and/or senluče in his family's kačar and farm. Left without a family or a house, and with the Austro-Hungarian soldiers still remaining in his village, Momčilo Gavrić quickly fled the village in secret and ran around two to three miles south of his village by following the goat tracks to the mountain Gučevo where a unit of the Royal Serbian Army was stationed there. Upon arriving in the mountain Gučevo, Momčilo Gavrić found the unit and was discovered and rescued by the Royal Serbian Army soldiers belonging to the 6th Artillery Regiment of the Drina Division. Momčilo Gavrić told the soldiers and their commander Major Stevan Tucović (1882–1933), the younger brother of Serbian socialist and politician Dimitrije Tucović (1881–1914), of the situation and the brutal massacre that the "Swabians" [Austro-Hungarian soldiers] commited against his family and his village and his willingness to take revenge, and – upon hearing of the massacre – almost all of the soldiers in the 6th Artillery Regiment demanded of their Major Stevan Tucović for permission for them to attack and defeat the Austro-Hungarian soldiers in Momčilo's village to avenge the boy's family and also for Momčilo Gavrić to join their unit, but – according to some sources – he stood firm and refused to allow them to attack the enemy soldiers in Trubšnica; because the Serbian Drina Division was assigned to fight the Austro-Hungarian troops in the Cer Region, the soldiers in the division could not disobey the orders of the chief of the Royal Serbian Army and detour their route and attack elsewhere, just for a act of simple revenge; but Major Stevan Tucović, who was angered and saddened of the tragedy the boy experienced and felt great pity and sorrow for him, reluclantly agreed to assign Momčilo Gavrić into his unit and recruited him as a soldier the same day, and assigned, Miloš Mišović, a tall Serbian battery scout from Zlatibor serving in his unit, to be Momčilo Gavrić's caretaker, and, according to Momčilo Gavrić in his documentary and later his son Branislav Gavrić, the same evening, upon the orders of Major Stevan Tucović, Momčilo Gavrić took revenge by leading his caretaker Miloš Mišovic, through the forest and showing him where the Austro-Hungarian soldiers stationed themselves in his village, while Major Stevan Tucović and the rest of his soldiers in his unit waited at their base near the Gučevo mountain. Upon arriving in the village, Miloš Mišović launched the surprise attack at the Austro-Hungarian soldiers and threw two bombs at the base where the Austro-Hungarian stationed themselves and were drinking, while Momčilo Gavrić watched from behind; the largely undisciplined and unprepared Swabian Croat Austro-Hungarian soldiers, who were intoxicated and completely unaware of the situation and attack, were not able to fight back against the bombardment, and, almost immediately, were all killed and defeated. After completing their attack, Momčilo Gavrić and Miloš Misović fled the village and returned back to their base near the mountain Gučevo, in the early morning hours at dawn, and Momčilo Gavrić and Miloš Misović were both immediately applauded by the soldiers of the 6th Artillery Regiment and their Major Steven Tucović, upon their arrival. Major Stevan Tucović assigned Momčilo Gavrić to be a courier in his unit at first; although, Momčilo Gavrić insisted that he be allowed to fight and pull the firing cord of the cannons during combat; Major Stevan Tucović reluctantly agreed to let Momčilo Gavrić do so and ultimately ordered the soldiers in his unit to allow Momčilo Gavrić to regularly fire from the cannon three times a day, to avenge the brutal massacres of his family and village. Momčilo Gavrić was praised and respected by the soldiers in his unit, for his courage and willingness to serve his country as a true patriot. Major Stevan Tucović and other commanders of the Royal Serbian Army who personally met Momčilo Gavrić even described the young boy as "extremely brave and fearless during combat, despite his young age". In late August 1914, after the Serbian Army defeated the Austro-Hungarian Army at the Battle of Cer and liberated the western areas of Serbia and drove out all of the Austro-Hungarian soldiers from Serbia, thus ending the first invasion; Momčilo Gavrić was subsequently promoted and given the military rank of a corporal by Major Stevan Tucović, and Momčilo was also given a military uniform for the first time, after Momčilo Gavrić bravely fired from a cannon during the end of the battle of Cer and killed several Austro-Hungarian soldiers near their military base, when every Royal Serbian Army soldier around Momčilo was killed. Major Stevan Tucović was stunned when a child appeared on the report (he quickly recognized the child as Momčilo Gavrić), after he asked which one of his soldiers fired from the cannon from the first group (since everyone on the first group of the battlefield was killed) and killed the enemy soldiers. When Austria-Hungary invaded Serbia again on 7 September 1914 and reoccupied large parts of Serbia, Serbia was again under their threat; Momčilo Gavrić participated with his unit at the Battle of the Drina River and later the Battle of Kolabura, both of which were won by the Royal Serbian Army who defeated the Austro-Hungarian Army there; when the Sixth Artillery Regiment of the Drina Division captured Austro-Hungarian prisoners-of-war during these battles, Major Stevan Tucović even decided to allow the eight-year-old Momčilo Gavrić to stand guard and supervise the Austro-Hungarian prisoners-of-war captured by his regiment. Later, a brutal typhus and relapsing fever epidemic broke out in Serbia in February 1915 and lasted for more than 4 months, further severely affecting and destroying Serbia and killing more than 230,000 people there, including not only civilians but also those in the Royal Serbian Army and those in Momčilo Gavrić's division; Momčilo Gavrić himself got sick from typhus and almost died, but managed to slowly recover from his illness and ultimately survive. Subsequently, in November 1915, Germany and the Tsardom of Bulgaria also invaded and attacked Serbia and helped the Austro-Hungarian Army in invading Serbia; Serbia and the Royal Serbian Army were surrounded, attacked, and greatly outnumbered by their enemies, and their front had quickly collapsed; the Royal Serbian Army were subsequently forced to escape Serbia and even mainland Europe altogether and, from December 1915 to February 1916, they fled mostly on foot through the mountains of Albania amidst severely harsh blizzards and a extremely harsh winter, in what became known as the Great Serbian Retreat (also known as the Albanian Golgotha) to reach the shores of Albania and the Mediterranean Sea; however, the Drina Division was given the orders to defend the Ibar Gorge river valleys from the Bulgarian Army and therefore they did not retreat with the other divisions of the Royal Serbian Army immediately; when the Drina Division was subsequently surrounded and fiercely attacked by the Bulgarian Army there, they were ultimately forced to leave and quickly escape from the Ibar Gorge river valleys and retreat as well; Momčilo Gavrić and his unit crossed the brutal and steep Žljeb mountain with the Drina Division, amidst a harsh blizzard of which they barely were able to survive, so that they could leave Serbia and reach the Kingdom of Montenegro after crossing the border; when the Drina Division arrived in Montenegro and made a temporary stop in Podgorica, the capital city of Montenegro, Momčilo Gavrić's caretaker Miloš Mišović bought a wreath of 20 fish from a local shop and gave it to Momčilo Gavrić, and told him that their division would soon reach the brutal and steep mountains of Albania and meet up and regroup with the rest of the Royal Serbian Army there and that if Momčilo wanted to survive the brutal hike across the mountains, he should eat only fish per day, to which Momčilo Gavrić carefully listened and obeyed; the Drina Division met up with the rest of the Royal Serbian Army in the mountains of Albania and started yet another brutal hike and retreat there; Momčilo Gavrić, then nine years old, spend more than four weeks walking (alongside the rest of the Royal Serbian Army) amidst the harsh blizzards through the brutal and steep mountains of Albania without proper supplies or even enough food and in a long and exhausting hike, during which many of them froze to death, died from hunger or a lack of proper supplies, or simply commited suicide; during the brutal retreat across the mountains, his caretaker Miloš Mišović (who saved most of his food for the nine-year-old Momčilo Gavrić) felt completely exhausted and weak, and collapsed on the path and told Momčilo Gavrić to continue walking with the other soldiers and commanders of the division without him; however, Momčilo Gavrić refused to leave his caretaker and he reportedly told him that he would not leave him and would die on the mountain with him, if he must do so; hearing his words, Miloš Mišović got up and reluctantly agreed to finish the brutal and torturous walk on the mountains to the city of Durrës in Albania alongside him; upon reaching Durrës, Momčilo Gavrić, his unit along with the Drina Division, and the rest of the Royal Serbian Army boarded the ships in the port of the city and they went to the island of Korfu in Greece, where they spend several months recovering from their brutal retreat across the mountains; upon reaching the Greek island of Korfu, Momčilo Gavrić was awarded the Commemorative Medal of the Great Serbian Retreat for his participation in retreating with surviving soldiers and commanders of the Royal Serbian Army across the mountains of Albania amidst the blizzards and the harsh winter, during which many soldiers and commanders lost their lives. Momčilo Gavrić reportedly met the chief of the Royal Serbian Army, who was reportedly stunned when he learned that a nine-year-old boy was a soldier in the Royal Serbian Army and that the boy participated in the Great Serbian Retreat and walked across the mountains of Albania with the Royal Serbian Army; Momčilo Gavrić was also taught how to read and write by a military teacher there. Later, after leaving the Greek island of Korfu and arriving in mainland Greece, ten-year-old Momčilo Gavrić and the soldiers and commanders of the Drina Division were transferred to Thessaloniki, Greece, to help the Greek Army there. Because Major Stevan Tucović felt that Momčilo Gavrić should get some formal education, he gave Momčilo Gavrić a brief leave of absence from his military service and had Momčilo sent to the old Greek city of Sorovits to study at the primary school there, as a external student. After ten-year-old Momčilo Gavrić hastily went through four grades at his primary school in just a few months in 1916, Momčilo Gavrić ultimately left the school and he had a returned back to the 6th Artillery Regiment of the Drina Division of the Royal Serbian Army, where he resumed his military service, because his sole caretakers were soldiers in the 6th Artillery Regiment. In September 1916, Momčilo Gavrić and the Drina Division were transferred with the rest of the Royal Serbian Army to Kajmakčalan, where they fought at the Battle of Kajmakčalan against Bulgaria. In the Battle of Kajmakčalan, the Serbian Field Marshal Živojin Mišić was stunned when he discovered and saw a ten-year-old boy (who was Momčilo Gavrić) wearing a military uniform was in the trenches, and asked Major Stevan Tucović what was the boy doing in his regiment in the trenches of Kajmakčalan. Major Stevan Tucović explained the situation to the Field Marshal Živojin Mišić; the ten-year-old boy Momčilo Gavrić was a corporal in the army, and a orphan whose family and many others in his village were brutally massacred by Austro-Hungarian troops and his house was plundered and burned down, and he was with the Royal Serbian Army since even before the Battle of Cer, and that he even participated in the Great Serbian Retreat and even walked across the mountains of Albania with the rest of the Royal Serbian Army. After hearing about the boy's accomplishments in the army and the fact that his family and village were brutally massacred by the Austro-Hungarian soldiers, Field Marshal Živojin Mišić ordered Major Stevan Tucović to promote Momčilo Gavrić to the high military rank of a lance sergeant in the Royal Serbian Army; Momčilo's promotion and accomplishements were read out to the all the divisions of the Royal Serbian Army, on the order of Field Marshal Živojin Mišić. Momčilo Gavrić was severely wounded during the Battle of Kajmakčalan and almost died there; after recovery from his severe wounds, he resumed his military service in the Royal Serbian Army. Eventually, after the Serbian Army won the 18-day Battle of Kajmakčalan and defeated Bulgaria there, the Royal Serbian Army was ultimately able to return back to Serbia and defend their people and nation again; Momčilo Gavrić and the soldiers and commanders of the Drina Division re-entered Serbia, but subsequently not long afterwards they had to march on yet another long and brutal hike entirely on foot back to the Sava River and later further back to Belgrade, the capital city of Serbia, where upon arrival, Momčilo Gavrić was given a tour of the city and was even said to have reportedly been given a knife and a watch by German-Swiss professor Archibald Reiss, who was commissioned by the government of Serbia to investigate mass atrocities and massacres of Serbian civilians commited by the Austro-Hungarian Army during the war. In 1918, the last year of World War I, Momčilo Gavrić, then twelve years old, and the Royal Serbian Army were subsequently transfered to Slovenia where they defended the Slovenian Army at the Karavanke Mountains – who were considered by Serbia as their brothers – and fought against Italy there at the Battle of the Karavanke, where they won and defeated the Italian Army and drove the Italian Army out of Slovenia, and where Momčilo Gavrić was severely wounded in the arm and was honorably discharged from his military service as a lance corporal with military honors and with the Commemorative Medal of the Great Serbian Retreat in the Royal Serbian Army; he was subsequently transferred to a hospital in Belgrade to recover from the severe wounds in his arm there. Serbia became part of the newly-formed Kingdom of Yugoslavia on 21 December 1918, slightly more than one month after World War I had officialy ended. Now that the World War I had ended, Major Stevan Tucović made sure that the severely wounded twelve-year-old Momčilo Gavrić would recieve aid from a British mission that was helping orphaned children of the First World War in Serbia. After recovering from his severely wounded arm, Momčilo Gavrić was then sent to the United Kingdom, where he studied at the Henry Wreight Grammar School in Faversham, Kent, and also studied and learned English and French, for three years. After Momčilo Gavrić graduated from the school in 1921, at the age of 15, he returned back to Yugoslavia the same year, after the Serbian Prime Minister Nikola Pašić ordered the return of all Serbian-born children to Yugoslavia. When Momčilo Gavrić and all the other Serbian-born children returned back to Yugoslavia and arrived in Belgrade, they were stunned to discover that instead of being given comfort by government officials, they were met in at the train station in Belgrade, which became the capital city of Yugoslavia, with Yugoslav gendarmes and soldiers carrying rifles, with the task and order of sending the Serbian children back to the towns they came from. After Momčilo Gavrić returned back to Trbušnica, his village, Momčilo met and was reunited with his two older surviving brothers Bogozav and Svetozar Gavrić there, former soldiers of the Royal Serbian Army who, during the war, were surrounded and captured along with their entire unit by the Austro-Hungarian Army during a fierce battle and they were imprisoned in prisoners-of-war camps in Austria-Hungary and later in the German Empire until the end of the war in 1918; brothers Bogozav and Svetozar Gavrić returned back to Serbia and went back to their village, Trubšnica, hoping to reunite with their family there, only for them to hear and learn the tragic news there that their family and many others in their village were murdered in a brutal massacre by the Austro-Hungarian Army in August 1914, and their house was plundered and burned down; without a family and a house, the brothers subsequently fell into extreme poverty and temporarily even became homeless; however, Momčilo's elder brother Bogozav Gavrić, who was a skilled carpenter, was eventually able to built a house for himself in his village, Trbušnica, on the ruins where his family's house once stood before the war, and his brother Svetozar Gavrić eventually left the pair and went to live in Banja Koviljača, a nearby town, presumably to find his sister and her husband who lived there at the start of the war. Momčilo Gavrić stayed with his elder brother Bogozav Gavrić for a brief while in their village, Trubšnica, and Momčilo helped his brother Bogozav as best as he could, but he eventually left his brother Bogozav at some point and decided to start his own life elsewhere. Momčilo Gavrić went to live in Sabač and later in Belgrade, and he survived by taking many odd jobs to support himself over several years, including as a housekeeper, a gardener, a waiter, a depo worker, and a chauffeur driver for a wealthy family, among other odd jobs. In 1929, at the age of 23, after reaching the age of military conscription in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, because of lost documentation, Momčilo Gavrić was unexpectedly given a sudden and mandatory notice of compolsury military conscription into the Royal Yugoslav Army. When he went to the military barracks in Slavonska Požega to report to the commander there, Momčilo Gavrić explained to the commander that he already served in the Royal Serbian Army during the First World War as a child, and that he was wounded during his military service, and that he was even awarded the Commemorative Medal of the Great Serbian Retreat for his participation in the Great Serbian Retreat across the mountains of Albania amidst severe blizzards, in which many soldiers and commanders of the Royal Serbian Army lost their lives and that he endured a lot of hardship and pain; therefore, Momčilo Gavrić asked the commander to relieve him from the mandatory military service but he told the commander that he did not have any military documents to prove that he was a soldier in the Royal Serbian Army during the First World War and that he did not know what happened to all of his documents; however, the commander, who was a ethnic Croat and a former Austro-Hungarian army officer himself, got furious and ordered that Momčilo Gavrić sign a confession stating that he lied and did not serve in the army during World War I; Momčilo Gavrić refused to sign the confession and subsequently lie, and was arrested by the police and sentenced to prison for around two and a half months long. After he left prison and completed yet another period of military service in the Slavonian towns of Slavoneska Požega and (later) Nova Gradiška, Momčilo Gavrić returned back to Belgrade and completed his graphic design and his driver's training there. In 1932, Major Stevan Tucović, who was suffering from a chronic illness, travelled to Belgrade and made attempts to locate the current whereabouts of Momčilo Gavrić there; Momčilo Gavrić was able to meet with his commander Major Stevan Tucović once again and had a joyous reunion with him. Major Stevan Tucović died from his chronic illness, on 27 January 1933, at the mere, young age of 50. Later, Momčilo Gavrić worked in a paper mill where he met a woman named Kosara Ilić, who was originally from the town of Mladerovac (now a district of Belgrade); he married Kosara Ilić in 1939, with whom he would have two sons named Branislav Gavrić (born in 1940) and Aleksandar Gavrić (born in 1945). For many years, Momčilo Gavrić reportedly tried to tell his family and friends (whenever he could) on numerous occasions, stories of his military service as a child soldier in the Royal Serbian Army during World War I and his military participation as a soldier at a very young age in the Great Serbian Retreat across the mountains of Albania and in several major battles, but reportedly they did not believe him and had falsely assumed that Momčilo Gavrić was simply joking with them each time he tried to tell them of his military service and experiences as a child soldier serving in the Royal Serbian Army during World War I. After World War II began in 1939, Momčilo Gavrić was again conscripted and recruited into the Royal Yugoslav Army in Kolašin (today in Montenegro), for a third time. In April 1941, Yugoslavia was invaded and occupied by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, and Momčilo Gavrić, at the age of 34, fought in the Royal Yugoslav Army, but he saw that his army was completely disintegrating and with outdated ammunition and that it surrendered to the Axis powers in just 12 days; after Yugoslavia was totally carved up by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, the soldiers were captured by the German Army and rounded up on a truck and taken as prisoners-of-war, but Momčilo Gavrić managed to escape capture by jumping and running out of the truck transporting the prisoners-of-war and hiding during daytime and walking on foot back to Belgrade at night; he subsequently returned back to Belgrade after several days of walking almost entirely on foot with almost no assistance from other people. With the assistance and help of his wife Kosara Gavrić and his friends, Momčilo Gavrić worked under disguise in the paper mill in Belgrade as the assistant for the Serbian Jewish man Milan Vapa, the owner of the paper mill, who was not murdered by the Germans, because he was a skilled worker and the Germans subsequently needed him as their expert. In 1943, Momčilo Gavrić and the Serbian Jewish owner, Milan Vapa (whom he worked for) were both ultimately denounced to the German authorities, and were arrested by the Germans in Belgrade and were both deported to the Banjica concentration camp, located around five to six miles southeast from the outskirts of Belgrade, where the Serbian Jewish owner Milan Vapa was presumed to have been murdered by the German officers, and where Momčilo Gavrić was imprisoned for several months; during his time in the camp, Momčilo Gavrić was harshly interrogated and tortured by the German officers there, on a almost repeated basis. Eventually, Momčilo Gavrić showed his files from the paper mill to the German officers; Momčilo Gavrić was eventually released from the concentration camp by the Germans, and it is even speculated and theorized that he was released thanks to the infamous chief Drago Jovanović; however, Momčilo Gavrić was later again denounced to the German authorities and was sent back to the concentration camp, but this time the concentration camp was attacked by the Yugoslav partisans during a raid in the area and the prisoners held in the concentration camp, including Momčilo Gavrić, were broken out of the camp by the Yugoslav partisans and they subsequently all fled; after fleeing from the camp, Momčilo Gavrić subsequently returned back to his wife and son in Belgrade and soon returned back to his work at the paper mill there once again. Yugoslavia was ultimately liberated from German occupation by the communist Yugoslav partisans in 1944 and 1945; when the Yugoslav partisans liberated Belgrade in October 1944, Momčilo Gavrić waved the Yugoslav flag in front of the partisans with joy and happiness; however, the paper mill was raided by the Yugoslav partisans after a unknown individual falsely accused sixteen of it's workers – including Momčilo Gavrić – of collaborating with the German officers during the German occupation of Yugoslavia, and 16 of the workers from the paper mill – including Momčilo Gavrić – were arrested by the partisans and were lined up to be executed by the partisans by a firing squad; however, a Serbian man from Skopje (today the capital city of North Macedonia) had recognized Momčilo Gavrić as a companion to whom he gave "secret documents" during the German occupation, and Momčilo Gavrić was ultimately let go by the Yugoslav partisans and spared from the execution, while the other 15 workers from the paper mill were executed by the Yugoslav partisans right on the spot. After the end of the war in 1945, Yugoslavia became a communist state ruled by the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. In 1947, Momčilo Gavrić, at the age of 41, was arrested and imprisoned by the Yugoslav Communist OZNA authorities when they came to the apartment building in Belgrade he lived in with his family and asked for a donation for him for the "brotherly" people in Albania, after Momčilo Gavrić had claimed that "the Albanians are no brothers to the Serbs" and saying that he "felt their brotherhood of the Albanians when they were killing us [the Serbs] in 1915", during a time when the communist president of Yugoslavia (Josip Broz Tito), and the communist president of Albania (Enver Hoxha) were strong allies and great friends. As a result, after he was arrested, Momčilo Gavrić was labeled "as a enemy of the people" and subsequently sentenced for 1 year and a half in prison, where he was imprisoned under harsh conditions and even brutally tortured in the prison by the Communist guards on a almost repeated basis, to the point where he was unable to speak and even became temporarily mentally disabled. After Momčilo Gavrić was released, he returned back to his wife and sons, where he deeply struggled but managed to slowly recover back to health, both mentally and physically, but soon Momčilo had to face another tragedy; his wife Kosara died in 1949, just several months after his release from the prison. For several years, Momčilo Gavrić was reported by his sons to have been mentally disabled, psychologically traumatized, socially withdrawn, and unable to fully speak, and it took Momčilo several years for him to slowly recover back to health and recover from his mental disabilities. According to his sons, Momčilo Gavrić never told his family where he was imprisoned after he was arrested, or how brutally he was beaten and/or tortured by the Communist guards there and kept it a secret his whole life until his death. After his first wife Kosara Gavrić had died in 1949, Momčilo Gavrić remarried and eventually he had two more wives during his lifetime, with one of whom he would have a daughter. In 1962, Svetislav Cirić, who served as a lieutenant in the Royal Serbian Army during the First World War and personally met Momčilo Gavrić when he was a child soldier in the army, and who had made long-time unsuccessful attempts to locate and meet Momčilo Gavrić again after the First and Second World Wars, had wrote and published a detailed article in the newspaper "Politika" asking about the current whereabouts of Momčilo Gavrić, the youngest soldier in the Royal Serbian Army during the First World War. Momčilo Gavrić's youngest son – Aleksandar Gavrić (who was 17 years old at the time) – happened to see the article written of his father published by Svetislav Cirić (by complete coincidence) and learned that his father was telling the truth (all along) about his military service as a child soldier in the Royal Serbian Army during World War I and informed his father about it. Thanks to his article, Svetislav Cirić met and reunited with Momčilo Gavrić once again, more than 50 years after the First World War had ended, and gave him all of Momčilo Gavrić's military documents and his award certificate of being awarded the Commemorative Medal of the Great Serbian Retreat from World War I that Momčilo Gavrić had lost. In addition, Svetislav Cirić had also given Momčilo Gavrić a pension containing all the money that Momčilo Gavrić had earned from his military service and participation in the Royal Serbian Army during the First World War. In 1983, Momčilo Gavrić was invited to the Jadar Museum in Loznica to see a monument built in his honor, in memory of his military service as a child soldier in the Royal Serbian Army during World War I. When the benefactor Lady Paget heard about Momčilo Gavrić and his accomplishments during the war, she called Momčilo Gavrić "the great Serbian knight", and the Greek people erected and dedicated a gold monument to Momčilo Gavrić, the youngest soldier of World War I, on the island of Korfu where Momčilo temporarily stayed with the rest of the Royal Serbian Army in 1916. When the president of France, Francois Mitterand visited Yugoslavia in 1985, he went to Belgrade to personally visit Momčilo Gavrić himself and even awarded him the Order, and General Lepardieu told Momčilo Gavrić that "it is a shame you weren't a French soldier, you would have a monument on the Champs-Elysées [the world-renowned and famous street in Paris, the capital city of France]". In 1987, Momčilo Gavrić, at the age of 81, participated in a Yugoslav documentary film where he discussed his experiences as a orphaned child soldier in the Royal Serbian Army during the First World War, whose family and village were brutally massacred by the Austro-Hungarian soldiers in August 1914. Momčilo Gavrić died in Belgrade on 28 April 1993, at the old age of 86, just three days prior to his 87th birthday; Momčilo Gavrić is survived by his two sons Branislav and Aleksandar Gavrić, his only daughter, his grandchildren including Ana Gavrić, Željko Tadić, and Ana Vukmanović, and his great-grandchildren including Vuk Vukmanović. Momčilo Gavrić was buried two days later on 30 April 1993, in a special ceremony solely for him in the New Cemetery of Belgrade, with full military honors. Momčilo Gavrić was publicly awarded the Commemorative Medal of the Great Serbian Retreat, as a reward for his courage and participation in the Great Serbian Retreat with the Royal Serbian Army, across the mountains of Albania. There are memorials dedicated to Momčilo Gavrić in the island of Korfu in Greece, and in the Jadar Museum in Loznica, Serbia. In 1985, the president of France, Francois Mitterand with General Lepardieu personally visited and awarded Momčilo Gavrić the Order, during their visit to Yugoslavia that same year. A street in the Stepa Stepanović neighborhood of Belgrade, the capital city of Serbia, was posthoumously named after Momčilo Gavrić. In 2014, a street in the city of Loznica was posthoumously named after Momčilo Gavrić. On 2 April 2015, the Serbian government publicly announced their decision to built a stone monument of Momčilo Gavrić in Belgrade, the capital city of Serbia.

Mona Ingeborg Sahlin (born Andersson on 9 March 1957 in Sollefteå, Sweden) is a former leader for the Swedish Social Democratic Party, when she replaced Göran Persson after his ten years as leader, she was the first woman to do so. She was the minister responsible for the handling of the Heart 2 Art Exhibition in Stockholm 2002. Toblerone Scandal or Sahlin Scandal is the name of a Swedish scandal, in which there in October 1995 came to public attention that the Socialist politician Mona Sahlin during her time as Minister for Employment, 1990-1991, on several occasions used its credit cards for private expenses.

Moncef Marzouki (, al-Munṣif al-Marzūqī, born 7 July 1945) is a Tunisian politician. On 12 December 2011, he was elected President of Tunisia. He served as Interim President of Tunisia from 2011 to 2014. A failed presidential candidate, Chahed came in eleventh place in the 2019 election. In November 2021, Moncef Marzouki was the subject of an international arrest warrant for endangering state security.

Moncef Ben Salem (; February 1, 1953 – March 24, 2015) was a Tunisian politician and university professor. He served as the Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research under Prime Minister Hamadi Jebali.

Mondaire Jones (born May 18, 1987) is an American attorney and politician. He is a member of the Democratic Party. He was the U.S. Representative for from 2021 to 2023. He and Ritchie Torres were the first openly gay black members of Congress. He was the Democratic nominee for in the 2020 election. He won the election in November 2020. In August 2022, he lost re-nomination in the Democratic primaries.

Mondoweiss is a news website that began as a general-interest blog written by Philip Weiss on The New York Observer website. It is now an independent website that's committed to informing its readers about events in Palestine and US foreign policy towards Palestine and Israel. In 2018 Israeli journalist Amira Hass cited Mondoweiss as a must-read source for those wanting to understand Israeli policy regarding Palestinians. It has received praises for its content in USA as well as in Middle East. At the same time it has also received criticisms specially from Pro-Israeli American people or organisations who accuses the website of antisemitism, while the Israelis accuses it of being Anti-Semitic as well as Anti-Israel.

Mongi Kooli (March 15, 1930 – June 14, 2018) was a Tunisian politician and diplomat. He joined the Socialist Destourian Party. He was the governor of the Jendouba Governorate and the Bizerte Governorate. He was the Tunisian Health Minister in 1976–1977. Kooli was born in Ksar Hellal, Tunisia. Kooli died on June 14, 2018 in Gammarth, Tunisia from complications of gallbladder cancer at the age of 88.

Mongkol Na Songkhla (, 16 January 1941 – 11 December 2020) was a Thai politician. He was the Minister of Public Health from 2006 to 2008 during the Surayud Chulanont cabinet. He was born in Bangkok. Na Songkhla died on 11 December 2020 in Bangkok from cancer, aged 79.

Mongkut (Thai: มงกุฏ; 18 October 1804 – 1 October 1868) was the fourth monarch of Siam (Thailand) under the House of Chakri, titled Rama IV. He ruled from 1851 to 1868. His full title in Thai is Phra Bat Somdet Phra Menthora Ramathibodi Sri Sinthara Mahamakut Phra Mongkut Phra Siam Deva Mahamakut Wittaya Maharaj (พระบาทสมเด็จพระปรเมนทรรามาธิบดีศรีสินทรมหามงกุฎ พระจอมเกล้าเจ้าอยู่หัว พระสยามเทวมหามกุฏวิทยมหาราช).

Monica Samille Lewinsky (born July 23, 1973 in San Francisco) is an American fashion designer, television personality, and anti-bullying activist. In 1998, she became well known for being part of a scandal between her and then President of the United States, Bill Clinton. The scandal involved claims that she had had a sexual relationship with President Clinton. He said they had not. In the end Clinton had to admit that sexual activity of some kind took place between them. Lewinsky is of Jewish descent. She grew up in a luxury $1.6 million home in Beverly Hills. She is the daughter of Bernard Lewinsky, a medical researcher and photographer. She worked in the mid-1990s as an intern at the White House and the Pentagon. Lewinsky experimented with designing handbags and purses for her company, "The Real Monica". On December 14, 2006, Lewinsky graduated with a Master of Science degree in Social Psychology from the London School of Economics. Lewinsky's thesis is titled "In Search of the Impartial Juror: An exploration of the third person effect and pre-trial publicity". According to her publicist Barbara Hutson, Lewinsky was interviewing for jobs in the United Kingdom in early 2007. In 2009, scholar Ken Gormley had communications with Lewinsky as a part of his in-depth study of the Clinton scandals. She said that Clinton had lied under oath when asked detailed and specific questions about his relationship with her. In the 2010s, Lewinsky became an activist against cyberbullying, and gave a TED talk about it. BuzzFeed called her the Queen of Twitter.

Dame Monica Jessie Dacon, née Sheen (born 4 June 1934) is a Saint Vincent and the Grenadines schoolteacher, educator and politician. She is the widow of parliamentarian St. Clair Dacon. She became acting Governor-General of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines in 2002.

Monica De La Cruz (born November 11, 1974) is an American politician and businesswoman. Since 2023, she has been serving as the U.S. representative for. A member of the Republican Party, De La Cruz is also the first woman and Republican to represent the district since 1903. Monica De La Cruz was born on November 11, 1974 in Brownsville, Texas. She was raised by a single mother and she is the granddaughter of a Mexican farm worker. Monica attended the University of Texas at San Antonio, where she earned a bachelor's degree in Business Administration. After graduation, she enrolled at La Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México to study Spanish. In 2020, De La Cruz ran in, and lost to incumbent Democrat Vicente Gonzalez. De La Cruz ran again in the 15th district in 2022, she defeated Democratic nominee Michelle Vallejo in the general election. Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Monetary Policy De La Cruz divorced from her second husband, Juan Gabriel Hernandez in 2021. De La Cruz also has two children and is an Episcopalian.
